tldr: **Where it goes:** servers the whole team needs go in the committed **`.mcp.json`** (project scope) with tokens written as **`${GITHUB_TOKEN}`**. Personal or experimental servers go in **`~/.claude.json`** (user scope, or local scope — the docs' default). **What the agent sees:** every server's tools at once (`mcp__server__tool`). **Detailed tool descriptions** stop it falling back to Grep, and **resources** (`@server:resource`) show what data exists without exploring. Use **community servers** for standard integrations and **custom** ones for team workflows. **What a tool returns on failure:** **`isError`** plus **errorCategory / isRetryable / a readable description**. Add a **customer-friendly** message for business rules. **Empty ≠ failed.** **Subagents retry transient errors themselves** and pass the rest up with partial results and what they tried.
mentalModel: MCP is the office's shared equipment. The equipment list pinned by the door (.mcp.json) is for everyone, and each person brings their own keycard (${VAR}). Your desk drawer (~/.claude.json) holds your own gadgets. A good machine has a clear label, or people keep using the old one they know (Grep). The catalogue on the wall (resources) saves opening every cupboard. When a machine fails, its display says **what's wrong and whether to try again**, never just “Error”.
whatItIs:
The exam guide covers integrating MCP servers into Claude Code and agent workflows (Guide §6 · TS 2.4, p.11) and returning
structured errors from MCP tools (TS 2.2, pp.9–10). The Claude Code and Agent SDK docs give the exact scopes, file locations
and error flag.

**Sub-concepts — each with its picture to remember**

| 3 | Local scope (docs' default) | A drawer in one office only. | 📘 docs only |
| 4 | `${VAR}` expansion | Each person brings their own keycard; the list never holds one. | ⭐ TS 2.4 · Knowledge 2 |
| 5 | Tools discovered at connection | Plug everything in and every machine is on the floor at once. | ⭐ TS 2.4 · Knowledge 3 |
| 6 | Rich MCP tool descriptions | A clear label, or people keep using the old machine they know (Grep). | ⭐ TS 2.4 · Skill 3 |
| 7 | Resources | The catalogue on the wall — no need to open every cupboard. | ⭐ TS 2.4 · Knowledge 4, Skill 5 |

| 9 | `isError` + errorCategory + isRetryable | The display says what's wrong and whether to try again. | ⭐ TS 2.2 · Knowledge 1–4, Skill 1 |
| 10 | Business-rule errors | “Needs a manager's approval” — said the way you'd tell a customer. | ⭐ TS 2.2 · Skill 2 |
| 11 | Empty ≠ failed | “No mail today” is not “the mailroom is locked”. | ⭐ TS 2.2 · Skill 4 |
| 12 | Local recovery in subagents | Jiggle the jammed printer yourself; escalate with what you tried and what you have. | ⭐ TS 2.2 · Skill 3 |

**MCP scopes** (docs; the guide names project and user)

| # | Aspect | Local (default) | Project | User |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Stored in | `~/.claude.json`, under this project's path | `.mcp.json` at the project root | `~/.claude.json` (top level) |
| 2 | Who gets it | Only you | Everyone who clones the repo | Only you |
| 3 | Which projects | This one | This one | All of yours |
| 4 | Committed to git? | No | Yes | No |
| 5 | Approval prompt | — | Yes, in interactive sessions (not in `-p` / SDK / cloud) | — |
| 6 | Precedence if names clash | 1st | 2nd | 3rd (then plugins, then claude.ai connectors) |
| 7 | Guide says use it for | — | ⭐ Shared team tooling | ⭐ Personal / experimental servers |

**Error kinds** (guide TS 2.2)

| # | Kind | Example | isRetryable | What the agent should do |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | transient | Timeout, service unavailable | true | Retry (in the subagent, bounded) |
| 2 | validation | Bad input | false (until the input is fixed) | Fix the input, don't repeat it |
| 3 | business | Refund over the limit | false | Explain it to the customer in plain words |
| 4 | permission | Account lacks access | false | Escalate / hand over with details |
| 5 | — (not an error) | Query ran, no matches | — | Answer “none found” |
howItWorks:
1. **Decide who needs each server.** The team → `.mcp.json` (committed). Just you → `~/.claude.json` (user or local scope).
2. **Keep secrets out of the file:** `"env": {"GITHUB_TOKEN": "${GITHUB_TOKEN}"}`. Each person sets the variable. If it's unset,
   Claude Code keeps the literal `${GITHUB_TOKEN}` text and shows a warning in `claude mcp list` (docs).
3. **Prefer community servers** for standard integrations (Jira, GitHub). Write a custom server for your team's own workflows.
4. **Make MCP tools win when they should:** describe what they can do that built-ins can't, what they return, and when to use them.
5. **Expose catalogs as resources** (schemas, doc trees, issue summaries). The agent — or you, with `@server:resource` — reads the
   catalog once.
6. **On failure, return `isError`** with errorCategory, isRetryable and a readable description, plus a customer-friendly message
   for business rules. Return **success with an empty list** when nothing matched.
7. **In subagents,** retry retryable errors locally. Pass everything else to the coordinator with **what you tried** and **what you
   already have**.

docsRefs.title: Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP — scopes, .mcp.json, env expansion, precedence, output limits
Common workflows — reference MCP resources with @server:resource
Give Claude custom tools — isError / is_error, errors keep the loop running

grounding.text: Three scopes: local (the default — ~/.claude.json under that project's path, only you, only this project), project (.mcp.json at the project root, checked in and shared with the team), user (~/.claude.json, all your projects, private to you).
Interactive sessions ask for approval before using project-scoped servers from .mcp.json; claude -p, Agent SDK and cloud sessions load them without asking.

When the same server name is defined in several places, Claude Code connects once using the highest-precedence definition: local, then project, then user, then plugin servers, then claude.ai connectors.

${VAR} and ${VAR:-default} expand in command, args, env, url and headers. If a variable is unset with no default the config still loads, claude mcp list shows a missing-variable warning, and the literal ${VAR} text is used.
In a remote server's url and headers, some credential variables (e.g. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, NPM_TOKEN) are read as empty rather than expanded.
MCP resources are referenced with @server:resource, which fetches the data from the connected server.
Claude Code warns when an MCP tool's output exceeds 10,000 tokens; the default maximum is 25,000 (MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS raises it).

A custom tool reports failure by returning isError: true (TypeScript) / "is_error": True (Python); the agent reads the message as an error and the loop continues. An uncaught exception also becomes an error result.

Scoping: project-level .mcp.json for shared team tooling vs user-level ~/.claude.json for personal/experimental servers; ${GITHUB_TOKEN}-style expansion keeps credentials out of the committed file; tools from all configured servers are discovered at connection and available together; resources expose content catalogs (issue summaries, documentation hierarchies, database schemas) to cut exploratory tool calls.

Skills: shared servers in .mcp.json with env-var tokens; personal servers in ~/.claude.json; detailed MCP tool descriptions so the agent doesn't prefer built-ins like Grep; community servers for standard integrations (Jira), custom servers for team-specific workflows; resources for catalogs.

The isError flag communicates tool failures; errors are transient (timeouts, unavailability), validation, business (policy violations) or permission; uniform "Operation failed" errors block good recovery; retryable vs non-retryable metadata prevents wasted retries.

Skills: return errorCategory, isRetryable and a human-readable description; retriable: false plus a customer-friendly explanation for business-rule violations; recover transient failures locally in subagents and propagate only unresolvable errors with partial results and what was attempted; tell access failures from valid empty results.

The guide names project and user scope; the docs add local scope (the default). The guide says all tools are discovered at connection; the docs also describe tool search and cached tool lists that defer connecting.
Putting the error metadata as JSON in the error's text content, and a customer_message beside the description, is this page's way of applying the guide's convention.
The servers, the fake community package names, the environment, the Grep-vs-MCP choice, the table catalog, the backends, their failures and the agent's reactions are invented.

examPoints.text: Scope: project-level .mcp.json for shared team tooling; user-level ~/.claude.json for personal/experimental servers.
Environment-variable expansion in .mcp.json (e.g. ${GITHUB_TOKEN}) manages credentials without committing secrets.
Tools from all configured MCP servers are discovered at connection and available to the agent at the same time.

examPoints.text: MCP resources expose content catalogs (issue summaries, doc hierarchies, database schemas) to cut exploratory tool calls.
Configure shared servers in project-scoped .mcp.json with env-var expansion for auth tokens.
Describe MCP tools' capabilities and outputs in detail so the agent doesn't prefer built-ins like Grep.
examPoints.lab: ✅ find_references description · ❌ J · playground “Descriptions vs Grep”

examPoints.text: Prefer existing community MCP servers for standard integrations (Jira); keep custom servers for team-specific workflows.
Expose content catalogs as MCP resources so agents see what data exists without exploratory calls.
The MCP isError flag communicates tool failures back to the agent.
Error kinds: transient (timeouts, unavailability), validation (bad input), business (policy violations), permission.
Uniform errors (generic “Operation failed”) stop the agent from choosing the right recovery.
Retryable vs non-retryable: structured metadata prevents wasted retries.
Return errorCategory (transient/validation/permission), an isRetryable boolean and a human-readable description.
For business-rule violations, mark them not retriable and include a customer-friendly explanation.
Recover transient failures locally in subagents; propagate only unresolvable errors, with partial results and what was attempted.
Tell access failures (need a retry decision) from valid empty results (a successful query with no matches).

labIntro:
Part 1: you write the team's **`.mcp.json`**, **your `~/.claude.json`**, and what your custom server exposes. The **simulated**
Claude Code starts a session for you **and for a teammate who just cloned the repo**, then an agent answers two questions with the
tools it sees. Part 2: you write the **MCP tool handlers** and the **orders subagent**. A simulated coordinator handles four
customer situations with them. Twelve mistakes, all from the exam guide (⭐).

variants.label: ✅ ⭐ scoped config with ${VAR}, rich descriptions, a catalog — and structured errors
variants.observe: team_server: a teammate gets github, jira and refund-platform, and the committed .mcp.json holds only ${GITHUB_TOKEN}/${JIRA_TOKEN}. personal_server: scratch-notes loads for you only. grep_preferred: the agent calls mcp__refund-platform__find_references → 7 callers across 4 services. catalog: one resource read. transient_timeout: 2 timeouts retried inside the subagent → 2 orders. policy_violation: 1 attempt, “Refunds over $500 need a manager's approval…”. empty_result: 1 query → “no orders on file”. access_failure: 1 query, the coordinator gets the permission error, the attempt and the profile → hands over with details.
variants.why: Each server lives in the scope matching who needs it, secrets stay in each person's environment, the agent can see what the MCP tool is better at and what data exists, and every error tells the agent what kind it is and whether trying again can help.

variants.label: ⭐❌ A — one generic “Operation failed” for every error
variants.observe: policy_violation: the agent can't tell a policy refusal from a glitch, retries 3× (3 refund calls) and tells the customer “Sorry, something went wrong.” transient_timeout: without isRetryable the subagent gives up after the first timeout, so the customer never hears about their orders.
variants.why: A uniform error hides what went wrong and whether retrying can help, so the agent can't pick the right recovery.
variants.fix: Return errorCategory, isRetryable and a human-readable description.

variants.label: ⭐❌ B — non-retryable, but only a machine code for the customer
variants.observe: One attempt (good) — but the customer is told “POLICY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED (code 4031)”.
variants.why: The agent passes on what it's given; a business-rule refusal needs a customer-friendly explanation.
variants.fix: retriable/isRetryable false plus a customer-friendly message.

variants.label: ⭐❌ C — “no orders” returned as an error
variants.observe: The query succeeds with no matches, but the tool reports isError “not_found”, retryable: the subagent queries 3 times, then the customer is told their order history couldn't be reached and is handed to a colleague.
variants.why: An empty result is a successful query; calling it an error triggers retries and escalation for nothing.
variants.fix: Return success with an empty list.

variants.label: ⭐❌ D — exceptions swallowed into an empty list
variants.observe: access_failure: the permission error becomes orders: [] and the customer is told “You have no orders on file with us.” — false. transient_timeout: the first timeout also becomes “no orders”.
variants.why: An access failure disguised as an empty result looks like a real answer; nobody decides to retry or escalate.
variants.fix: Return isError with the category; keep “empty” for successful queries only.

variants.label: ⭐❌ E — no local retry in the subagent
variants.observe: The first timeout (retryable) goes straight to the coordinator: the customer is handed to a colleague although the service answers on the third try.
variants.why: Transient failures should be recovered inside the subagent; only what it can't resolve goes up.
variants.fix: Retry retryable errors locally (bounded), then propagate.

variants.label: ⭐❌ F — propagate a bare “failed”
variants.observe: The coordinator gets {"status": "failed"} with no error, no attempts and no profile. It dispatches the subagent again (2 more backend calls in total) and tells the customer “Sorry, something went wrong. Please try again later.”
variants.why: Without the error, what was attempted and the partial results, the coordinator can't decide what to do next.
variants.fix: Propagate the structured error, the attempts and the partial results.

variants.label: ⭐❌ G — a literal token in .mcp.json
variants.observe: Everything connects — and the committed .mcp.json contains github.env.GITHUB_TOKEN as plain text.
variants.why: .mcp.json is checked in; anything in it is shared with everyone who can read the repo.
variants.fix: "GITHUB_TOKEN": "${GITHUB_TOKEN}" — each person sets the variable in their own environment.

variants.label: ⭐❌ H — the team's server in your ~/.claude.json
variants.observe: It works for you. A teammate who clones the repo loads only jira and refund-platform — no GitHub.
variants.why: User scope is private to you; shared team tooling belongs in the project's .mcp.json.

variants.label: ⭐❌ I — your experiment in the shared .mcp.json
variants.observe: scratch-notes now loads for every teammate (and asks each of them to approve it).
variants.why: Personal and experimental servers belong in user scope, not in the team's config.
variants.fix: Put it in ~/.claude.json (user scope) — or local scope for one project.

variants.label: ⭐❌ J — a one-line MCP tool description
variants.observe: The agent uses Grep and reports 3 callers — this repository only (one is a test). The other 4 services are missed.
variants.why: With “Finds references.” the agent can't see why the MCP tool beats the built-in it already knows.
variants.fix: Describe capabilities and outputs in detail, and say when to use it instead of Grep.

variants.label: ⭐❌ K — no resource catalog
variants.observe: The agent calls list_tables and then describe_table 6 times — 7 calls to find one table.
variants.why: Without a catalog the agent can only discover what exists by exploring.
variants.fix: Expose the schema catalog as an MCP resource.

variants.label: ⭐❌ L — a home-made Jira server
variants.observe: It connects — and the team now owns a custom Jira integration the simulation flags as a standard one.
variants.why: For standard integrations an existing community server is the default; custom servers are for team-specific workflows.
variants.fix: Use the community server; keep custom servers for things like refund-platform.

distractors.name: A · One generic error
distractors.fails: The agent can't choose: it retries a policy refusal and gives up on a timeout.

distractors.name: B · Machine code, no customer text
C · Empty result as an error
E · No local retry
distractors.fails: A 2-second blip becomes a human handover.
distractors.instead: Retry transient errors in the subagent.

distractors.name: F · Propagate a bare “failed”
distractors.fails: The coordinator re-dispatches blind and gives up.

distractors.name: G · Literal token in .mcp.json
distractors.fails: The secret is in git history for everyone.

distractors.name: J · One-line MCP tool description
distractors.fails: The agent sticks with Grep and misses other repos.
distractors.instead: Describe capabilities, outputs and when to prefer it.

distractors.name: K · No resource catalog
distractors.fails: Seven calls to find one table.
distractors.instead: Expose the catalog as a resource.

distractors.name: L · Custom server for Jira
distractors.fails: You maintain what a community server already does.
distractors.instead: Community for standard; custom for team-specific.

rows: Any of 1–4 with a generic error

experiments: Run ✅ on all eight scenarios and compare what you and the teammate load.
In ✅, move scratch-notes into PROJECT_MCP and run personal_server — that's ⭐❌ I.
In ✅, shorten find_references' description to one sentence and run grep_preferred: how short can it get before Grep wins?
Run ⭐❌ D on empty_result and on access_failure: the customer hears the same words. Which one is true?
In ✅, change range(1, 4) to range(1, 3) and run transient_timeout: 2 timeouts, 2 attempts — what happens?

questions.q: The team wants all 25 developers to get the same GitHub MCP server as soon as they clone the repository. Each developer has a personal access token, and last quarter a token committed in a config file had to be revoked. What is the right configuration?
opts: A project-level .mcp.json in the repository, with the token referenced as ${GITHUB_TOKEN}.
Each developer's user-level ~/.claude.json, set up from an onboarding document with their own token.
A project-level .mcp.json that holds one shared service token, so developers don't need their own.
A CLAUDE.md section explaining how to add the GitHub server, which Claude follows at session start.
questions.explain: A project-scoped .mcp.json is version-controlled, so everyone gets the server. Environment-variable expansion keeps each person's token out of the repository. B works, but it isn't shared and drifts from developer to developer. C commits a secret, which is exactly what went wrong last quarter. D is not how servers are configured.

questions.q: A developer wants to try an experimental MCP server that nobody else uses and that may be removed next week. The project's .mcp.json is reviewed by two teammates on every change, and a server added there would load for all 25 developers. Where should the experimental server be configured?
opts: In the project's .mcp.json, with a note in the pull request saying the server is experimental and optional.
In a feature branch's .mcp.json, merged to main only if the experiment is still going after a week.
In their user-level ~/.claude.json, which applies only to them.
In the root CLAUDE.md, as an instruction for Claude to connect to the server whenever the developer asks.
questions.explain: Personal or experimental servers belong in user scope (~/.claude.json), where they affect nobody else. A and B put an experiment into the team's shared configuration. D: Claude doesn't connect to servers based on CLAUDE.md instructions.

questions.q: Your MCP server offers find_references, which searches all 30 service repositories and returns call sites with the owning team. Its description is “Finds references.” In 50 logged sessions the agent used Grep, which sees only the current repository, 46 times, and missed callers in other repositories in 12 of them. What is the best fix?
opts: Remove Grep from the agent's tools, so that find_references is the only search tool available to it.
Describe find_references in detail: what it searches, what it returns, and when it beats Grep.
Add a CLAUDE.md line telling the agent to prefer MCP tools over built-in tools for every search task.
Rename find_references to grep_all_repos, so the model sees it as a better version of the Grep tool.
questions.explain: An MCP tool with a thin description loses to a familiar built-in tool. Describing its capabilities in detail (scope, outputs, when to prefer it) fixes the choice. A removes a tool that is still the right choice for local searches. C is a blanket rule that is wrong for local searches. D renames without explaining.

questions.q: Before answering any question about the analytics database, the agent makes about 12 describe_table calls to discover which tables and columns exist, adding roughly 40 seconds per question. The schema changes about once a month. What is the best way for the MCP server to cut this exploration?
opts: Merge describe_table into a single describe_all_tables tool that returns every table's schema in one call.
Paste the full schema into the system prompt by hand, and update it whenever someone notices a change.
Cache describe_table results on the server, so each of the 12 exploratory calls returns more quickly.
Expose the schema catalog as an MCP resource, so the agent can see what data exists without tool calls.
questions.explain: MCP resources expose content catalogs, such as a database schema, so the agent knows what is available without exploratory tool calls. A still needs a call on every question and returns everything. B goes stale silently. C makes the unnecessary calls faster instead of removing them.

questions.q: The team needs Claude to read and update Jira tickets, and separately to run the company's own deployment-approval workflow, which exists nowhere else. One engineer proposes building custom servers for both “to keep everything consistent”. How should they source the MCP servers?
opts: Build custom servers for both as proposed, so that the team controls all of the code and all of its conventions.
Use an existing community Jira server, and build a custom server only for the in-house approval workflow.
Use community servers for both, adapting the closest community workflow server to the approval process.
Skip MCP for the approval workflow, and describe its steps in CLAUDE.md for Claude to follow by hand.
questions.explain: Use existing community servers for standard integrations like Jira, and reserve custom servers for team-specific workflows. A rebuilds something that already exists. C forces a generic server onto a unique process. D replaces a tool with instructions the model has to follow.

questions.q: A developer has both a GitHub MCP server and a Jira MCP server configured. To “let Claude use both”, a colleague proposes a wrapper that connects to one server, disconnects, and connects to the other when needed, which would take about two days to build. How should you evaluate the proposal?
opts: Worth building, since Claude Code can hold a connection to only one MCP server at any one time.
Worth building, but only if the two servers expose tools with the same names that would otherwise clash.
Unnecessary: tools from all configured servers are discovered at connection and available together.
Unnecessary, because Claude Code merges the two servers into one combined server at start-up.
questions.explain: Tools from every configured MCP server are discovered at connection time and are available at the same time. A and B rest on a limit that doesn't exist. D gives the right verdict for an invented reason: the servers stay separate. Their tools are simply all available.

questions.q: process_refund returns isError with the text “Operation failed” for every failure. When a refund exceeds the policy limit, the agent retries it four times and then tells the customer to “try again later”. This affects about 70 conversations a week. What should the tool return for this case?
opts: The same error text, plus a retry limit of one enforced by the agent loop to cut the wasted attempts.
A generic “please contact support” message that the agent can pass on to the customer word for word.
A success response with a zero amount, so that the agent moves on without retrying the refund again.
A business-rule error marked not retryable, with a customer-friendly explanation of the policy limit.
questions.explain: Structured error metadata (category, retryability, explanation) lets the agent respond correctly: don't retry, explain the limit, and offer the right next step. A cuts the retries, but the agent still doesn't know why the refund failed. B is a generic status that hides the reason. C reports a failure as success.

questions.q: A customer gives the date “next Tuesday”, and lookup_order rejects it because it expects YYYY-MM-DD. The tool returns isError with “Invalid input”, and in 60% of these cases the agent apologises and asks the customer to phone instead. Which error response lets the agent recover on its own?
opts: isError with errorCategory “validation”, isRetryable true, and a description of the expected date format.
isError with errorCategory “transient”, so that the agent retries exactly the same request after a short delay.
An empty result list, so the agent asks the customer for more details about which order they mean.
isError with the date parser's full stack trace, so the agent can see exactly where parsing failed.
questions.explain: A validation error that says it is retryable and gives the expected format tells the agent exactly how to fix the input and try again. B mislabels the error, so the identical bad input is retried. C disguises a failure as an empty result. D is noise that doesn't say what input is expected.

questions.q: An order-lookup tool catches every exception and returns an empty list. During a 25-minute database outage, the agent told 140 customers they had no orders, and several cancelled their subscriptions. What is the core design error?
opts: The agent should have retried every empty result a few times before telling the customer anything.
The database should have had a replica, so that the outage would never have reached the lookup tool.
The system prompt should tell the agent to doubt empty results and ask customers to confirm their orders.
The tool merges access failures with empty results, so “couldn't check” looks like “nothing found”.
questions.explain: An access failure must be reported as an error, not as a valid empty result. Otherwise the agent cannot tell the two apart. A retries genuine empty results as well. B addresses availability, not the misleading response. C asks the model to doubt a signal that the tool itself made misleading.

questions.q: A research subagent's source API times out on about 5% of calls, and most timeouts succeed on a second try. Every timeout is currently passed straight up to the coordinator, which restarts the whole subagent and discards up to 10 minutes of completed work. What is the best design?
opts: Have the subagent catch timeouts and return an empty result marked successful, so that the run continues.
Pass every error up with more detail, so that the coordinator can decide faster whether to restart the subagent.
Retry transient failures in the subagent; pass up only unresolved errors, with partial results and attempts.
Raise the source API's timeout from 10 to 60 seconds, so that far fewer of the calls time out at all.
questions.explain: Recover locally from transient failures, and pass up only what can't be resolved, together with partial results and what was tried, so the coordinator can decide well. A hides the failure. B still restarts for errors that one retry would have fixed. D slows every call to paper over the occasional timeout.

questions.q: A shared .mcp.json references ${GITHUB_TOKEN}. A new developer hasn't set that variable, and the GitHub tools fail to authenticate on their first day. They ask whether Claude Code refused to load the config. What does Claude Code do, and what is the robust setup?
opts: It loads the config, warns about the variable and uses the literal text; document it, and default non-secrets.
It refuses to start until every variable is set; commit a default token so that new developers can begin.
It silently drops the whole server; move the token into the committed .mcp.json so that the server always loads.
It prompts for the value at start-up and stores it, so new developers only need to answer the first prompt.
questions.explain: Per the docs, a missing variable produces a warning and the literal ${…} text is used, so the server loads but authentication fails. Document the variable, and give non-secret settings a ${VAR:-default}. B and C commit secrets and describe behaviour that doesn't happen. D invents a prompt.

faq.q: The guide mentions two scopes; the docs have three. Which is right?
faq.a: Both. The guide contrasts project (.mcp.json) with user (~/.claude.json). The docs add local scope — the default when you run claude mcp add — which is also in ~/.claude.json but only for the current project. Local and user are both private to you.

faq.q: Does ${VAR} work in a remote server's headers?
faq.a: Yes, ${VAR} expands in command, args, env, url and headers. But the docs note that some credential variables (e.g. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, NPM_TOKEN) are read as empty in a remote server's url and headers. That's why this lab passes tokens through a local server's env.

faq.q: Are errorCategory and isRetryable part of the MCP protocol?
faq.a: The protocol-level flag is isError (is_error in the Python SDK). errorCategory, isRetryable and the description are the guide's recommended structure for the error's content, so the agent can decide what to do.

faq.q: Are all MCP tools really loaded at the start?
faq.a: The guide says tools from all configured servers are discovered at connection and available together. The docs add tool search and cached tool lists, which can defer connecting a server until first use. For the exam, go with the guide.

faq.q: What about very large tool outputs?
faq.a: Claude Code warns above 10,000 tokens of MCP tool output; the default limit is 25,000 (MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS raises it). A resource catalog or a tool that returns only what's needed is usually the better fix.

playgroundIntro:
Pick where each server lives and how your tools report failures, then see what happens: what you and a teammate load, which tool
the agent picks, and what the customer is told. It all runs on the **simulated** session, agent and backends.

playground.label: ⭐ Scopes & secrets
playground.mentalModel: The list by the door is for everyone; bring your own keycard; your drawer is yours.
playground.meaning: Where each server lives, how its token is written, and what a teammate who clones the repo gets.
playground.docs: mcp § scopes, env expansion; guide TS 2.4 Knowledge 1–2, Skills 1, 2, 4
examples: Start a session for me and for a teammate.
tryThis: GitHub in user or local scope: the teammate has no GitHub.
Literal token: flagged in the committed file.
Teammate hasn't set GITHUB_TOKEN: a missing-variable warning, no GitHub.
scratch-notes in project scope: everyone gets it.

playground.label: ⭐ Descriptions vs Grep
playground.mentalModel: A clear label, or people keep using the old machine they know.
playground.meaning: The agent must find callers across all services. Your MCP tool can; Grep can't.
examples: Find every caller of process_refund across our services.
tryThis: vague: Grep → 3 callers, this repo only.

playground.label: ⭐ Resources
playground.mentalModel: The catalogue on the wall saves opening every cupboard.
playground.meaning: The agent must find one table among many.
tryThis: With the catalog: one resource read.

playground.label: ⭐ Error metadata
playground.mentalModel: The display says what's wrong and whether to try again.
playground.meaning: How your tools report failures, across four situations.
playground.docs: guide TS 2.2 Knowledge 1–4, Skills 1–2; agent-sdk/custom-tools § Handle errors
examples: I'd like a $900 refund on ORD-2002.
tryThis: generic on policy: 3 attempts, “Sorry, something went wrong.”
code only on policy: the customer sees the code.
generic on timeout: gives up after one try.

playground.label: ⭐ Empty vs failure
playground.mentalModel: “No mail today” is not “the mailroom is locked”.
playground.meaning: A customer with no orders, or a service that refuses access — and how your tool reports each.
tryThis: empty + error: 3 queries and a pointless handover.
permission + swallow: “You have no orders” — false.

playground.label: ⭐ Local recovery
playground.mentalModel: Jiggle the jammed printer yourself; escalate with what you tried and what you have.
playground.meaning: What the orders subagent does before, and when, it hands a failure to the coordinator.
tryThis: timeout + no local retry: a handover for a blip.
permission + no partial info: a blind re-dispatch, “try again later”.
